positive.scenario: The team ships the same onboarding checklist widget as a native module in the iOS app, the Android app, and the web dashboard, all built from one shared spec. A support ticket showed the 'skip for now' button wasn't persisting the skip choice across sessions on iOS, so the fix adds a local-storage write after the skip tap. The Android and web versions have the identical bug since they were cloned from the same original implementation. The engineer wants to know how to track which platforms still need the equivalent fix applied.

negative.scenario: A developer maintains three microservices that all expose a '/health' endpoint, each written independently by different teams over the years with different frameworks and response shapes. They're updating the Go service's health check to also ping a new downstream dependency, purely because that service alone added the dependency. The Python and Node services don't have this dependency and their health checks were never meant to mirror each other's internals. The developer just wants to note the change in that service's own changelog.

adversarial.scenario: While closing out a ticket about slow query timeouts, an engineer bumps the database connection pool timeout constant in the primary backend config and writes a one-line commit message referencing the ticket number. It later turns out this same backend framework was forked wholesale to produce the internal admin-tools service and the customer-facing kiosk service, both still sharing the exact same connection-pooling module verbatim. The engineer closes the ticket without checking those two, assuming a config tweak in one repo is too minor to matter elsewhere. Nobody records anywhere whether the same timeout issue exists, or was addressed, in the other two deployments.
